sm: The Army planned to detonate nearly five tons of aging lead azide explosives at its ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, around nine this morning, and asked nearby residents to leave because wind could carry toxic lead dust. Officials said foam barriers and gel blocks would absorb the blast, and the Environmental Protection Agency sent teams and mobile labs across three states. A federal appeals court lifted its hold on the permit on Monday. Other news: hackers broke into a system the CIA shares with the Director of National Intelligence, though no classified information was taken. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced a crackdown on scammers, saying more than eight billion dollars in losses were stopped and over 800 people charged. Senators including Tom Cotton and John Kennedy raised questions about Nvidia, Jensen Huang's return as CEO, and Commerce Department export controls on AI chips to China.

Ambassador Mike Huckabee said the Israel aid agreement still runs two more years and likely cannot end abruptly without Congress acting. Gaza saw a funeral for a senior Hamas leader killed in an Israeli strike. The show then turned to Washington Wednesday with political scientist Hunter Baker. The hosts cited polling that 55 percent of voters said government corruption was crucial to their vote, and a Gallup finding that 89 percent believe corruption is widespread. Baker said Trump's push to reinstate Jensen Huang looks bad and everyone moved too fast, though Huang denies Trump was decisive. They also discussed House Democrats' large majority and the elevation of Sarah McBride to a leadership post, which Baker called a deliberate message.

Baker said he reads Abdul El-Sayed's challenge to Chuck Schumer as elevating the Israel issue, and that there is little ideological diversity left in either party, partly because of social media and narrow primaries. He noted that pro-life Democrats who would support legal limits have all but vanished. On Texas, Democrats won four state Supreme Court seats, and incoming Chief Justice Maggie Ellis wants to revisit a rule letting judges decline to perform weddings that conflict with their faith. Baker argued religious freedom exists to help people live together peacefully, and said the left wants professionals to participate rather than simply ensuring services are available. A Thanksgiving lightning round followed. Baker chose turkey, cornbread dressing, canned cranberry sauce, sweet potatoes without marshmallows, and pumpkin pie with Cool Whip.

Baker named macaroni and cheese as the most overrated side, said politics at the Thanksgiving table should be prohibited, and said he is thankful his daughter came home from college with her fiancé. World Tour then covered child marriage in Germany. A state report in Baden-Württemberg found more than 350 marriages involving minors over fourteen years, some girls as young as eleven. About 40 percent involved Syrian families, and less than one percent involved native Germans. A woman named Özlem described being married at thirteen to a man of thirty-two. A counseling center representative said girls face years of control and violence tied to family honor, and Heritage Foundation researcher Simon Hankinson said such practices fade only with assimilation, with education as a first step.

The counseling center representative described counseling a seventeen-year-old in secret about her rights. Germany's 2024 law refuses to recognize any marriage involving a minor under sixteen, even one conducted abroad, but many girls do not press charges for fear of retribution. A lighter item covered England's spoof Turnip Prize for the worst modern art made with the least effort. Finalists include a leek with memory sticks attached and a traffic jam made of toy cars and a jar of jam. Then a profile of young adult novelist Nadine Brandes, who wrote A Time to Die, about a world with clocks counting down to each person's death. She waited years for publication, believing God closed doors until it was time to write. Her research included walking a high wire, riding a train across Russia, rock climbing, and cooking cattails.

Brandes also worked as a cook on a sailboat and got seasick. She has seven young adult books, and her four children love to help her write. Commentator Janie B. Cheney then spoke about the family dinner table. She noted how often the TV family in Heartland fights at the table yet keeps returning to it, and said political arguments at holiday meals and eating on the run threaten the custom. Cheney said cooking and setting a proper table is worth the effort, citing her son hosting dinners after his divorce and philosopher Roger Scruton's view of the table as a symbol of homecoming. She closed with Deuteronomy twelve seven, saying God's invitation to eat before him still stands. Tomorrow's show will cover girls' sports ballot initiatives and giving praise on Thanksgiving.
